title: Supreme Court to Decide Whether Trump Can Bar Asylum Claims at Southern Border
excerpt: The justices took up the administration's appeal on Friday after two lower courts held the categorical asylum ban unlawful. Arguments come in the next few months; a ruling is due by the end of June.
body:
• The US Supreme Court agreed on Friday, November 13, to decide whether President Donald Trump's proclamation barring asylum claims at the southern border is legal. Arguments are expected in the coming months, with a ruling due by the end of June.
  • Two lower courts held the categorical ban unlawful: a federal judge found Trump lacked the sweeping authority he asserted, and the D.C. Circuit upheld that ruling in April while letting the policy stay in effect during the appeal.
  • The ban applies to people arriving at the US-Mexico border. It does not change work, student or family visa routes — including H-1B, F-1 or green-card processing — which are not part of this case.
  • Nothing changes at the border today: the appeals court's stay means the administration can keep applying the policy while the Supreme Court hears the case.

The US Supreme Court agreed on Friday to consider the legality of President Donald Trump's restrictions on access to asylum at the US-Mexico border, taking up one of the central policies of his immigration crackdown. The justices granted the administration's appeal of lower-court rulings that found Trump exceeded his authority by denying migrants caught entering the country illegally the chance to apply for asylum, according to Reuters. Arguments are expected in the coming months and a ruling by the end of June.

Who is affected — and who is not

The policy covers people who arrive at the southern border. Under it, migrants caught crossing illegally are barred from pursuing asylum claims, and the bar also reaches some people who present at official crossings without certain medical or criminal-history information. It is not a change to employment, student, tourist or family immigration: visa categories used by most Indian applicants are outside the proclamation and outside this case. What is at stake is whether a president can switch off the asylum system Congress wrote into immigration law for one border, by proclamation.

What the policy does

Trump announced the curbs hours into his second term, on January 20, 2025, in a proclamation that described the situation at the border as an invasion. The restrictions — and the fast-track deportation procedures they are meant to enable — are written to remain in effect until the president determines the invasion has ended. Immigrant rights groups sued on behalf of would-be asylum seekers who said they were denied a credible-fear interview, the screening meant to test whether a person would face persecution at home on grounds such as race, religion, nationality, group membership or political opinion.

The administration's argument, as the Justice Department put it to the court, is that presidents have inherent authority to secure the border and protect national security, and that because granting asylum is discretionary, the president can decide broadly who is eligible to seek it. The counterargument rests on the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows anyone in the country or at an official port of entry to apply for asylum. A federal judge in Washington ruled for the challengers in July 2025, finding Trump lacked the sweeping authority he asserted; the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld that ruling in April 2026 but kept it from taking effect while the administration appealed, according to USA Today.

The wider docket

The case joins a term already heavy with immigration disputes. The justices are separately due on December 9 to hear arguments over deporting migrants to countries other than their own without a chance to show the harm they may face, and they will also decide whether the administration can detain immigrants without a chance to seek bond. In June, the court backed the government's authority to turn away asylum seekers when officials judge border crossings too overburdened to handle more claims, and in September it let third-country deportations resume. Reuters notes the court, with its 6-3 conservative majority, has been largely deferential to Trump on immigration in his second term.

What happens next

Briefing and arguments will run into the new year, with a decision expected by the end of June, when the term closes. Until then, the stay left in place by the appeals court means the asylum bar continues to operate. A ruling for the administration would confirm a broad presidential power to suspend asylum access; a ruling against it would restore the lower courts' holding that the categorical ban exceeds the president's authority.
